{{Short description|American physicist (born 1965)}}

'''Joseph Jacobson''' (born June 28, 1965 in [[Newton, Massachusetts]]), is a tenured professor and head of the Molecular Machines group at the Center for Bits and Atoms at the [[MIT Media Lab]], and is one of the inventors of microencapsulated electrophoretic display<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Jacobson|first1=Joseph|title=An electrophoretic ink for all-printed reflective electronic displays|journal=Nature|volume=394|date=18 May 1998|issue=6690|pages=253–255|doi=10.1038/28349|bibcode=1998Natur.394..253C|s2cid=204998708}}</ref> (known as [[E Ink]]) commonly used in electronic devices such as [[e-readers]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Tu|first1=Chau|title=How Electronic Ink Was Invented|url=https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/how-electronic-ink-was-invented/|website=sciencefriday.com|access-date=14 March 2017}}</ref>  He is the founder of several companies including [[E Ink Corporation]], Gen9, Inc., and [[Kovio]], and serves on the scientific board of several more companies (such as Epitome Biosystems).

==Education and career==
Jacobson received an [[bachelor's of science|Sc.B.]] in [[physics]] at [[Brown University]] and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in physics at the [[MIT|Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. He was a postdoctoral research associate at [[Stanford University]] in experimental and theoretical nonlinear non-local quantum systems. While at Stanford, he set the world record for the shortest pulse ever generated by a laser (in optical cycles).

Jacobson first had the idea for the e-book in 1993, while working on his [[postdoctoral research]] in [[quantum mechanics]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Digital Ink |author=Charles Platt |url=https://www.wired.com/1997/05/ff-digitalink/ |work=Wired Magazine |date=May 1997 |access-date=13 June 2012}}</ref>

In 1997, Jacobson along with [[JD Albert]], [[Barrett Comiskey]], Russ Wilcox and Jerome Rubin founded E Ink Corporation.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Klein|first1=Alec|title=A New Printing Technology Sets Off a High-Stakes Race|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB946939872703897050|website=wsj.com|date=4 January 2000 |access-date=14 March 2017}}</ref>

In 1999, MIT's Technology Review named Jacobson as one of the [[TR35|TR100]], one of the most influential inventors under the age of 35.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?TRID=574 |title= Innovators under 35 |last1=  |first1=  |last2=  |first2=  |year= 1999 |work= MIT Technology Review |publisher=  |access-date= January 26, 2013 |archive-date= March 15, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160315084817/http://www2.technologyreview.com/tr35/profile.aspx?trid=574 |url-status= dead }}</ref> He invented [[nanoparticle]]–based ink that can print on a flexible computer processor using an inkjet printer.<ref name="BookerBoysen2005">{{cite book|last1=Booker|first1=Richard|last2=Boysen|first2=Earl|title=Nanotechnology for dummies|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_flVj1rz6CQC&pg=PA135|access-date=2 September 2010|date=25 July 2005|publisher=For Dummies|isbn=978-0-7645-8368-1|page=135}}</ref>  He was awarded the [[Gutenberg Prize of the International Gutenberg Society and the City of Mainz]] in 2000. In 2001, he received a Discovery magazine award for technological innovation. In 2002, he received a [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]] Collegiate Inventors Award. In 2013 Jacobson received the [[Wilhelm Exner Medal]].<ref>[https://www.wilhelmexner.org/medalists/joseph-m-jacobson/ ''Joseph M Jacobson''], retrieved on 20 March 2020 in Wilhelmexner.org</ref> On 5 May 2016, Jacobson was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame for his work in developing E Ink.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Primozec|first1=Ursa|title=Interview with Barrett Comiskey, father of electronic ink|url=https://www.visionect.com/blog/interview-with-barrett-comiskey/|website=visionect.com|date=27 May 2016 |access-date=14 March 2017}}</ref>
